tagline: Follow the river north through mining country toward limestone caves
intro: The North Pend Oreille Scenic Byway follows SR 31 from Tiger to the Canadian border, paralleling the river and railroad before curving through lake country north of Metaline Falls. State of Washington Tourism gives the drive as 27 miles and one hour. Part of the International Selkirk Loop, the byway is promoted by that organization for solitude in the Selkirk Mountains. At Metaline Falls, Selkirk peaks rise more than 1,000 feet above the river within a mile of town, and Washington Rock towers beside the crossing.

The corridor was part of the Pend O’Reille Highway, a state road established in 1923 to connect Spokane with the border. When Washington renumbered its highways in 1964, the Newport-to-border section became SR 31. The number’s southern reach shortened in 1973, when SR 20 extended to Newport and took over the stretch south of Tiger.

Start at Tiger’s junction of SR 20 and SR 31, then head north through Ione beside the Pend Oreille River. At Metaline, the highway crosses the river into Metaline Falls beneath Washington Rock. Beyond town, repeated curves lead past Crescent and Boundary lakes toward Washington’s easternmost border crossing. Gardner Cave in Crawford State Park is a separate excursion near this northern end.

moments.title: Tiger
moments.text: Tiger began as a river landing established by George Tiger in 1899, on the west bank of the north-flowing Pend Oreille. The surviving store and post office dates from 1913 and now houses the Tiger Historical Center and Museum. It is the only building remaining from the community. The museum opens seasonally at the junction where SR 31 leaves SR 20 and the byway begins.
moments.notice: The museum occupies Tiger’s surviving 1913 store and post office.

moments.title: Metaline Falls
moments.text: In 1942, the FBI arrested George Kubota, Sr., a member of the Japanese-American family that ran a hardware store in Metaline Falls, and imprisoned him in Spokane. The local newspaper’s editors and most town residents protested his arrest and vouched for the family’s loyalty. The FBI eventually released him, and the family was not sent to an internment camp.

moments.title: Gardner Cave
moments.text: Gardner Cave formed in Cambrian-age Metaline Limestone and contains stalactites, stalagmites, flowstone and a column two feet in diameter. The limestone passage extends 1,055 feet into the ground. Ed Gardner, a local bootlegger, claimed to have found it in 1899 when the earth collapsed beneath him and his horse. Gardner stored moonshine underground, using the cave’s constant 39-degree Fahrenheit temperature. William Crawford deeded the cave and 40 acres to Washington State Parks in 1921. The cave lies inside Crawford State Park, where tours offer a close view of the limestone formations.
moments.notice: Stalactites, stalagmites and flowstone decorate the cave.
